system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

- Some items list "forbidden_terms": words a previous rewrite kept that point to the area or the source. Use none of
  them, nor any synonym or morphological variant of them; describe the thing in generic words instead.
Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:6413f7e9c981",
  "problem": "How to find out when and why misalignment emerges during training rather than only evaluating final models.",
  "did": "Proposed evaluating a progressive series of training checkpoints and auditing training environments for rewarding cheating, hacking or deception.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "evaluating only final or released models"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Checkpoint evaluation gives independent signal on when and how training should be adjusted to avoid misalignment.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "feature",
   "learn",
   "reward"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:c8d71138d5b3",
  "problem": "Whether the mathematical model of inoculation, in particular the assumption of constant contextual generalization factor k, holds empirically.",
  "did": "They built a controlled toy setting with GPT-4.1 mini and measured the effect across 32 trait/oversight/instruction combinations to estimate k.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "To gain more control over the traits exhibited by the oversight and test the theory's strongest assumption.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "generalization",
   "model"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:2c485213a28a",
  "problem": "Whether attacks learned against one accessible model carry over to other models.",
  "did": "They trained on individual models, such as the open-weight GPT-oss-20b alone, and measured how the attacks transferred to the other targets.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "optimizing a weighted sum of rewards across multiple models"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Training on less robust models may give a useful intermediate signal for attacking more robust ones.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "robust",
   "transfer"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:a410db4d205e",
  "problem": "How strongly to interpret the LLM-as-a-Judge's strong average performance as evidence for the method.",
  "did": "They cautioned against reading the results as an endorsement of relying solely on LLM judges, since the judge fails on lies that depend on private knowledge and fact-checking.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The HP-KR truthfulness hinges on the assistant's actual knowledge, which is hard for an external judge to infer, and future judges may not fact-check reliably.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "caution",
   "knowledge"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:7fe32db45777",
  "problem": "How closely clean data must match the poison",

  "alternatives_named": [

   "Open-Platypus",

   "modern names for the same birds"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To test how closely the clean examples must match the poisoned data to trigger homeopathic learning.",

   "trigger",
   "unrelated"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:7a16df44a39c",
  "problem": "How to prevent the jailbreak investigator from reward hacking by satisfying the affirmative-prefix target without producing actually harmful output.",

  "alternatives_named": [
   "targeting only the affirmative response string"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To alleviate reward hacking, i.e. to check that responses are actually harmful.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "meeting",
   "string"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:fa713e31e1c1",
  "problem": "Whether to count a tailored many-shot jailbreaking prompt that worked better on SSC as a legitimate result.",

  "alternatives_named": [
   "a tailored prompt with examples of decoding other Base64-encoded constraints"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The tailored setup assumes the auditor already knows how to construct and decode such constraints, which is unrealistic.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "benchmark",
   "knowledge"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:5ad1f30514c3",
  "problem": "Which risk areas and activities embedded evaluators should prioritize given limited scope and expertise.",
  "did": "Focused on four areas tied to the Hugging Face incident that fit Transluce's expertise in model behavior evaluation, and excluded cybersecurity controls and work duplicating others.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "a comprehensive list of risks",
   "improving cybersecurity controls on agent swarms",
   "duplicating METR's frontier risk reports"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "They are not cybersecurity experts and want to complement rather than duplicate ongoing activities.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "embedded",
   "matching"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:836999a53f7c",
  "problem": "Testing whether future adversaries could evade the auditor, given that the evaluated attacks were not designed against it.",
  "did": "They tried distraction-based evasion attempts themselves, and discussed other possible evasions (more covert steganography, clean-label backdoors, jailbreaking the auditor) without evaluating them.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "more covert steganography",
   "clean-label backdoors",
   "semantic backdoor triggers",
   "datasets that jailbreak the auditor itself"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "An adversary may construct datasets that cannot be understood by the auditor or that distract it, so detection metrics alone do not establish robustness.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "detection",
   "detector",
   "robustness"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:5585ddf9e6f5",
  "problem": "Choosing a held-out evaluation for the decoder that tests generalization to unseen user attributes.",
  "did": "Finetuned on 78 of 80 SynthSys attributes and held out \"gender\" and \"age\" for evaluation.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Evaluating on held-out attributes tests question-answering ability beyond the finetuning distribution.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "adaptation",
   "distribution",
   "generalize"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:d4a6567d931a",
  "problem": "How to interpret the flag rate of the LLM monitor on open-test original benchmarks, where ground truth is not known to be non-cheating.",
  "did": "They manually examined some flagged transcripts, found most were genuine cheating attempts, and so treated the flag rate only as an upper bound on the false positive rate.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Most manually examined flagged transcripts were indeed cheating, via test modification and special-casing, so the flags are not all false positives.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "detector",
   "false"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:68603702a152",
  "problem": "How to treat LLM unreliability (hallucination, false positives) when assessing attacker viability.",
  "did": "They argued that failures only proportionally reduce attacker value rather than preventing deployment, and that false-positive validation cost will fall as models improve.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Developing and monetizing exploits tolerates failures, since a 1% or 10% failure rate only reduces potential value by that fraction.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "adversary",
   "preventing"
  ]
 }
]
